summary: Specifies extensions to the Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback for codec control messages, helpful in conversational multimedia with central mixers. They cover things such as requesting a fresh video frame or limiting bit rate. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5104 adds RTCP messages that let a receiver or mixer ask an RTP media sender to refresh video, adjust encoding, or limit its bit rate. The messages are negotiated for a session and must be used with congestion control.

subtitle: RTCP feedback messages for requesting video refreshes, encoding trade-offs, and temporary rate limits.

tldr.problem: The RTP feedback profile needed additional messages for conversational multimedia, especially conferences using centralized mixers. Traditional signaling can take too long for controls tied to a live media stream.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5104 adds six RTCP feedback messages for refresh requests, temporal-spatial trade-offs, H.271 back-channel data, and temporary bit-rate limits. Session Description Protocol (SDP) advertises support using the ccm feedback value.
tldr.outcome: The messages let participants request changes over the media path, while still requiring congestion control and protection against forged feedback. RFC 5104 is updated by RFC 7728 and RFC 8082.

today: RFC 5104 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7728 and RFC 8082. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Add Codec Control Messages
sections.content:
The Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback (AVPF) supports RTCP-based feedback, but its original focus was point-to-point and small multipoint calls without centralized control. RFC 5104 adds feedback useful in conversational multimedia with Multipoint Control Units (MCUs), including mixers and translators.

The messages travel in RTCP on the media path because their value falls as delay increases. The RFC limits their purpose: they relate to an RTP stream or codec, use simple binary formats, and rely on AVPF timing rules to avoid flooding the network.
sections.plainLanguage: These messages let people and mixers make timely requests about a live media stream. They are limited to media control, rather than serving as a general session-control system.

sections.title: Six New RTCP Feedback Messages
sections.content:
RFC 5104 defines six messages. TMMBR requests a temporary maximum media bit rate, and TMMBN reports the sender's current limiting requests. FIR asks a sender for a decoder refresh point. TSTR requests a temporal-spatial trade-off, and TSTN reports the trade-off the sender will use. VBCM carries an H.271 video back-channel message.

TMMBR and TMMBN use the RTPFB packet type, value 205, with FMT values 3 and 4. FIR, TSTR, TSTN, and VBCM use PSFB, value 206, with FMT values 4, 5, 6, and 7. In the common feedback header, the media-source SSRC field is set to zero; target senders are identified in each message's control information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a defined purpose, such as asking for a fresh video picture or reporting a rate limit. Its packet type and format value tell the receiver which request or report it carries.

sections.title: Requesting a Decoder Refresh Point
sections.content:
A Full Intra Request (FIR) is a command to the media sender. On receiving it, the sender MUST send a decoder refresh point as soon as possible, subject to congestion control. A refresh point resets the decoder to a known state.

Each FIR entry identifies its target sender and carries an 8-bit sequence number. A new command increases the number by one modulo 256, while a repeated command keeps the same number. FIR is not for reacting to lost pictures; the RFC recommends Picture Loss Indication for that case. It gives a new conference participant joining and a switching MCU changing streams as examples where FIR may be useful.
sections.plainLanguage: FIR tells a sender to provide a new decoder refresh point as soon as it can. It is for cases that need a fresh picture, not as the response to ordinary picture loss.

sections.title: Requesting a Temporal-Spatial Trade-Off
sections.content:
A Temporal-Spatial Trade-off Request (TSTR) suggests how an encoder should balance spatial quality and frame rate. Its Index ranges from 0 to 31: zero indicates the highest possible spatial quality, and 31 the highest possible temporal resolution. The values express a preference, not exact quality or frame-rate measurements, and the sender decides what it can support.

The sender replies with a Temporal-Spatial Trade-off Notification (TSTN), carrying the value it will use. The chosen value may differ from the request. The notification identifies the request sequence number; if several requests from one requester are pending, the sender responds to the highest sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: TSTR suggests a balance between picture quality and frame rate. TSTN tells the requester what setting the sender will actually use.

sections.title: Temporary Maximum Bit-Rate Requests
sections.content:
A receiver, translator, or mixer sends a Temporary Maximum Media Stream Bit Rate Request (TMMBR) to ask a sender to limit a stream. The request includes a maximum total media bit rate and measured per-packet overhead. The sender returns TMMBN with the bounding set: the most limiting tuples it has received, together with their owners.

The bit rate uses a 6-bit exponent and 17-bit mantissa, with the value calculated as mantissa * 2^exp. The measured-overhead field is 9 bits and reports a running average. The sender must send TMMBN after a TMMBR naming it, even when that request does not change the bounding set.

A TMMBR limit cannot exceed the maximum negotiated during session setup. Increasing a limit does not replace congestion control; the sender must wait after announcing an increase so other receivers can report stricter limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver reports the highest rate it can handle, including packet overhead. The sender shares the requests that currently set the strictest limits, but congestion control still governs sending.

sections.title: Carrying H.271 Video Feedback
sections.content:
The Video Back Channel Message (VBCM) carries a feedback bit string defined by ITU-T Recommendation H.271 from a receiver toward a sender. An entry identifies the target SSRC, has a sequence number, gives a payload type and length, and carries the variable-length octet string with padding to a 32-bit boundary.

The RFC cautions that some H.271 messages overlap with native AVPF or RFC 5104 messages, and that not all H.271 message types are safe for multicast or centralized multipoint use. Implementations must respect congestion control and should prefer the corresponding IETF-native message when it has the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: VBCM carries codec-specific feedback in an RTCP message. The receiver and sender need to understand the H.271 payload, and the RFC restricts its use in multipoint situations.

sections.title: Congestion, Security, and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
All modified sending behavior must respect congestion control. For example, a refresh point can contain many packets, so the sender must pace it even if that delays recovery. A false TMMBR can force a low rate, forged TMMBN can misstate who owns a limit, and repeated FIRs can make video jerky.

The RFC calls for authentication and integrity protection of setup signaling and feedback. It identifies the SAVPF profile, which combines Secure RTP and AVPF, as one way to protect feedback. In mixer arrangements, separate security contexts and filtering can isolate participants.

Support is negotiated with the media-level SDP rtcp-fb attribute and the ccm value. Parameters identify fir, tmmbr, tstr, or vbcm support. The answerer removes unsupported parameters and cannot add new ones; only the intersection of the offer and answer may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Feedback can change a sender's behavior, so it must be protected against forgery and still follow congestion control. Before using a message type, both sides must advertise support for it in SDP.
